extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers, cultural critics, and intellectuals interested in education, morality, and social criticism (Victorian-era public)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and standards for what 'culture' ought to be and how to judge people, institutions, and societies by their contribution to human perfection and harmonious growth. The page sets normative criteria (virtues, motives, anti-patterns) for cultural life rather than a procedural rubric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Culture as the study of perfection
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture is properly described as having its origin in the love of perfection; it is a study of perfection and 'the endeavour, also, to make it prevail.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arnold contrasts two motives for culture (curiosity vs love of perfection) and emphasizes the latter as the primary ground for true culture. Culture should aim at 'making reason and the will of God prevail' and at 'an inward condition' of mind and spirit rather than outward circumstances. The passage stresses growth and becoming ('not a having and a resting, but a growing and a becoming') as the character of perfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Culture combines scientific passion and the passion for doing good
rubrics_metrics.description: True culture is 'possessed by the scientific passion, as well as by the passion of doing good' — it seeks knowledge and also seeks to diminish human error and misery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Culture must balance desire to 'see things as they are' (intellectual curiosity) with moral/social impulses to act for others' benefit. Arnold warns that the passion for doing good can be overhasty and substitute crude conceptions for reason; culture corrects that by grounding action in careful thought and wide experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfection as an inward, harmonious, and general expansion
rubrics_metrics.description: Perfection consists in 'an internal condition, in the growth and predominance of our humanity proper... in the general harmonious expansion of those gifts of thought and feeling which make the peculiar dignity, wealth, and happiness of human nature.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perfection is not material circumstance but an inner state. It requires harmonious development of all faculties (no over-development of one power at expense of others) and must be communal — the individual must 'carry others along' in the march toward perfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject treating machinery (wealth, railroads, coal, population, religious organisations) as ends
rubrics_metrics.description: Things like wealth, machinery, population, bodily health, and institutions are 'machinery' and should not be mistaken for ends or constituting true greatness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arnold gives many anti-pattern examples: seeing coal or railroads as the basis of national greatness, equating wealth with spiritual greatness, or treating bodily vigor as an end divorced from spiritual aims. Culture's role is to 'dissipate delusions' and set spiritual standards of perfection that subordinate such machinery to higher ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sweetness and light as the characters of culture's ideal
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture (and poetry) aim at 'sweetness and light' — beauty, harmony, and the human nature perfected on all sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arnold invokes Greek art and poetry as paradigms where religion and poetry unite to produce beauty suffused with devout energy. The ideal is to combine aesthetic sensibility with moral strength; lacking either undermines the full ideal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish genuine curiosity from frivolous curiosity
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a laudable curiosity — 'a desire after the things of the mind simply for their own sakes' — and a futile, diseased curiosity which is mere vanity or social distinction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genuine curiosity furthers scientific passion and culture; the shallow 'curiosity' that amounts to a smattering of classical learning as a class badge is an anti-pattern. Arnold cites Montesquieu: study should 'augment the excellence of our nature.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Make reason and the will of God prevail (culture's teleology for action)
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture should aim to 'make reason and the will of God prevail' in actions and institutions rather than acting impulsively or on crude conceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arnold stresses that acting or instituting is of little use unless based on reason and a true moral aim; culture tempers enthusiasm for action with thoughtful assessment and broader knowledge to avoid premature or ill-founded reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral discipline and sincerity ('do what he knows') as a cultural virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: The discipline by which man rescues life from thrall is 'To walk staunchly by the best light one has, to be strict and sincere with oneself, not to be of the number of those who say and do not, to be in earnest.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Culture preserves and values Hebraic discipline (earnestness, honesty in action) alongside Hellenic appreciation of beauty. This ethical earnestness enables practical effectiveness and final moral worth; Arnold argues it remains an 'eternal possession.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use culture to judge institutions by the ideal of complete human perfection
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture applies its standard — the idea of complete and harmonious human perfection — to test religious organisations, political movements, and social practices, exposing narrowness and inadequacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arnold uses criticism of Puritanism and contemporary religious newspapers as examples: acknowledge the good they have done (moral discipline) but judge their narrow ideal against the broader ideal of sweetness and light; culture's criticism is 'resolutely testing these organisations by the ideal of a human perfection complete on all sides.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Culture must not neglect the subduing of animality (moral virtues)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultured people have often failed 'in the necessary first stage to perfection, in the subduing of the great obvious faults of our animality,' and morality is indispensable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arnold warns that aesthetic or intellectual refinement without moral discipline leaves culture incomplete; both artistic ideal and Puritan virtue have roles and failures — a genuine cultural ideal requires both moral rectitude and aesthetic breadth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oppose the conception of culture as mere classical smattering or class badge
rubrics_metrics.description: The disparaged 'culture' of a smattering of Latin and Greek is often mere vanity, social distinction, or pedantry, and is not true culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arnold criticizes views (e.g., Mr. Bright, Frederic Harrison) that reduce culture to 'a desirable quality in a critic of new books' or 'small fault-finding.' True culture is broader and morally engaged; beware the anti-pattern of treating classical learning as an elitist badge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance knowledge and action; avoid acting without sound knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture remembers that 'acting and instituting are of little use, unless we know how and what we ought to act and to institute.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This standard cautions reformers and social actors: practical zeal must be informed by thought and broad knowledge. The passion to do good must be tempered by the scientific passion to understand before acting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Culture's role in clarifying standards of greatness and beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture helps fix 'standards of perfection that are real' and prevents confusing material success with true greatness; greatness is a spiritual condition 'worthy to excite love, interest, and admiration.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use culture to question popular measures of national greatness (wealth, coal, industry) and re-center evaluation on what will evoke lasting admiration — e.g., Elizabethan spiritual effort versus recent material prosperity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfection requires promoting the development of others (the social obligation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Perfection, as culture conceives it, 'must be a general expansion' — individuals must 'carry others along with him in his march towards perfection.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultural development is communal; isolated individual improvement is incomplete. Arnold frames this as consonant with religion's injunctions ('to promote the kingdom of God is to increase and hasten one's own happiness') and as a corrective to egotistic individualism.
